#### Asset pricing tests {#sec-fama-macbeth}
 
A long-short return is one summary of whether asset growth predicts the cross-section of returns. A complementary view comes from Fama-MacBeth regressions [@fama.1973], which estimate the average risk premium associated with a characteristic after running cross-sectional regressions period by period. [tidyfinance]{.pkg} implements the standard procedure in `estimate_fama_macbeth()`, which takes a panel and a model formula, fits one cross-sectional ordinary least squares (OLS) regression per period, and aggregates the period-level coefficients into average risk premia with Newey-West standard errors with automatic lag selection.

Here, we winsorize the AG signal at the 1st and 99th percentiles to keep extreme observations from dominating the cross-sectional regressions and pair it with log market capitalization as a size control.
 
```{r}
#| label: fama-macbeth-data
fm_data <- sorting_data |>
  drop_na(asset_growth, mktcap_lag, ret_excess) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  mutate(
    asset_growth = winsorize(x = asset_growth, cut = 0.01),
    log_mktcap = log(mktcap_lag)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```
 
```{r}
#| label: fama-macbeth-fit
fm_results <- estimate_fama_macbeth(
  data = fm_data,
  model = "ret_excess ~ asset_growth + log_mktcap"
)
```
 
```{r}
#| label: tbl-fama-macbeth
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Fama-MacBeth regression of monthly excess returns on lagged asset growth and lagged log market capitalization. Coefficients are time-series averages of monthly cross-sectional OLS estimates; standard errors are Newey-West [@newey.1987] with automatic lag selection. The intercept and slopes on the right-hand-side variables are reported on the monthly scale. Sample: ", sample_years(fm_data), ".")'
#| echo: false
fm_results |>
  mutate(
    factor = recode(
      factor,
      "intercept" = "Intercept",
      "asset_growth" = "Asset growth",
      "log_mktcap" = "Log market cap"
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Variable = factor,
    `Risk premium` = risk_premium,
    SE = standard_error,
    `$t$~statistic` = t_statistic,
    `N (months)` = n
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 4,
    escape = FALSE,
    format = "latex",
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = ""
  )
```
 
The negative slope on `asset_growth` in @tbl-fama-macbeth lines up with the long-short evidence in @tbl-univariate-sort-ag and @tbl-customized-comparison: high-AG firms earn lower subsequent returns, conditional on size. As an external benchmark, @cooper.2008 [Table III, Panel A, Model 1] reports a Fama-MacBeth slope on annual asset growth of -0.0922 ($t$~statistic of -6.52). Converted to a monthly basis, their slope is approximately `{r} round(-0.0922 / 12, 4)` $(=-0.0922/12)$, directly comparable to the magnitude of the AG coefficient in our table.[^cooper-fm-controls] Switching to `vcov = "iid"` or supplying `vcov_options = list(lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)` would change the standard-error treatment without altering the rest of the call, and adding additional regressors (e.g., a beta estimate from `estimate_betas()`, a profitability measure, an idiosyncratic-volatility control) is a one-line extension to the model formula. The same function therefore covers the standard cross-sectional asset-pricing test that complements the portfolio-sort evidence used throughout the rest of the paper.

[^cooper-fm-controls]: @cooper.2008 additionally controls for book-to-market and 6- and 36-month past returns, both negatively correlated with AG.


## Summary and discussion {#sec-summary}

Empirical asset pricing depends on dozens of construction choices that no consensus pins down. [tidyfinance]{.pkg} makes those choices first-class objects in the workflow: each is an argument, each has a documented default, each can be varied without rebuilding the pipeline. Disagreements over construction become empirical questions, not implicit assumptions buried in code.

We will maintain and extend the package on CRAN. At the time of writing, all functions are covered by comprehensive unit tests, with code coverage reported at 100% by [Codecov](https://app.codecov.io/gh/tidy-finance/r-tidyfinance), and each release is accompanied by passing R CMD check results across multiple operating systems, including the latest macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu environments. The companion Hugging Face artifacts (the spliced risk-free rate and the precomputed factor library) are refreshed on a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow, so the published series track new WRDS releases without manual intervention.

Companion materials at [tidy-finance.org](https://tidy-finance.org) integrate [tidyfinance]{.pkg} into open coursework and self-study tracks for graduate finance and asset pricing in [R]{.proglang}. The site also hosts a reviewed channel through which researchers can publish replications and new construction routines, so the catalog of factors and conventions can grow with the literature rather than freezing at the package's release.

## Computational details {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: renv-versions
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
renv_lock <- jsonlite::fromJSON("renv.lock")
pkg_version <- function(pkg) {
  v <- renv_lock$Packages[[pkg]]$Version
  if (is.null(v)) {
    v <- tryCatch(
      as.character(utils::packageVersion(pkg)),
      error = function(e) NA_character_
    )
  }
  v
}
r_version <- renv_lock$R$Version
```

We obtained the results in this paper using [R]{.proglang} `{r} r_version` with the following packages: [tidyfinance]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("tidyfinance")`, [dplyr]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("dplyr")` [@dplyr], [tidyr]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("tidyr")` [@tidyr], [ggplot2]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("ggplot2")` [@ggplot2], and [lubridate]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("lubridate")` [@lubridate]. We install development versions of [tidyfinance]{.pkg} with [pak]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("pak")` [@pak]. Figures additionally use [ggforce]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("ggforce")` [@ggforce], [scales]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("scales")` [@scales], and [patchwork]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("patchwork")` [@patchwork]. CRAN hosts [R]{.proglang} and all packages at [https://CRAN.R-project.org/](https://CRAN.R-project.org/). [renv]{.pkg} `{r} pkg_version("renv")` [@renv] ensures full reproducibility of the computational environment. Reproducing the factor return data requires an institutional subscription to WRDS, as the underlying CRSP and Compustat data are proprietary and cannot be redistributed. A pseudo-data path with identical schema is available via `download_data(domain = "pseudo", ...)` for readers without WRDS access; see @sec-data-download.

Reproducing this manuscript takes about 15 minutes: `quarto render jss-manuscript.qmd` uses the WRDS subset described in @sec-data-download, or pseudo data of identical schema for readers without WRDS access. Timings reported here are obtained on `{r} sessionInfo()$running` with a `{r} parallel::detectCores()`-core processor running [R]{.proglang} `{r} r_version`; WRDS extracts are not pre-cached, so the 15-minute figure includes the time to download the underlying CRSP and Compustat panels.

We publish all code, data workflows, and documentation at [https://github.com/tidy-finance/jss-multilingual-factor-library](https://github.com/tidy-finance/jss-multilingual-factor-library). The code is released under the MIT License, which is compatible with the GNU General Public License (GPL).
